tests.title: Original General Training diagnostic: everyday life, work and community repair

texts.title: Meadowbank Community Centre: a guide for visitors
paragraphs: The Meadowbank Community Centre welcomes visitors of all ages. You do not need to be a member to enter the building or use its public reading room. Annual membership costs £18 and is available to residents aged sixteen or over. It lasts twelve months from the date of registration, rather than ending in December. Members receive reduced prices for selected classes. Please show your membership card before paying; discounts cannot be applied afterwards. A replacement for a lost card costs £3.

Places on classes can be booked up to six days in advance, either online or at reception. Telephone bookings are not accepted. To receive a full refund, cancel at least twenty-four hours before the class starts. Later cancellations are not refunded unless the centre cancels the session. If a class is full, ask reception to add you to its waiting list. Staff contact people on the list by email when a place becomes available; a place is not automatically reserved for them.

The swimming pool is currently closed while damaged tiles are replaced. There is no confirmed reopening date. During this period, the upstairs studio offers additional chair-based exercise and beginner art sessions. No previous experience is required for either activity. Art materials are included in the advertised fee, but exercise participants should bring their own towel.

The café is open to everyone from Monday to Friday, between nine in the morning and four in the afternoon. Food is not allowed in the studios or reading room. Water in a closed bottle is permitted throughout the centre.

The main entrance has three steps. Visitors who require step-free access should use the entrance on the east side, where there is a ramp and an automatic door. Reception can provide a large-print activity leaflet on request.

texts.title: Riverside Festival: shuttle travel information
paragraphs: A temporary shuttle will connect Northgate railway station with the Riverside Festival on Saturday 18 July. It is intended to reduce traffic near the festival field, where public car parking is unavailable. The first shuttle leaves the station at 8.30 a.m. Services then run every twenty minutes until 11.30 a.m. From noon, they run every thirty minutes. The last return journey leaves the festival at 7 p.m. These times apply to the festival shuttle only, not to regular town buses.

A return ticket costs £4 for adults and £2 for children aged five to fifteen. Children under five travel free when accompanied by a fare-paying adult. Tickets can be bought from the driver using a bank card; cash is not accepted on the shuttle. A festival admission ticket does not include transport. Keep your shuttle ticket for the return journey.

At Northgate station, the shuttle departs from Bay C, beyond the taxi rank. Do not wait at the usual town-bus stop outside the main station doors. Staff wearing orange jackets will direct passengers between the station exit and Bay C. The shuttle stops once on the outward journey, at Hillview Library. It does not stop there on its return to the station. The journey normally takes twenty-five minutes, but road conditions may increase this. Allow additional time if you are catching a train.

Every vehicle has one space for a wheelchair. Passengers who need this space are advised to reserve it through the festival office by Thursday 16 July. Booking a wheelchair space is free, but the usual passenger fare still applies. Folding pushchairs may be carried in the luggage area. Large suitcases and bicycles cannot be carried. Dogs are not permitted, except assistance dogs. Any passenger who needs help boarding should tell the driver before the vehicle starts to load other passengers.

Heavy rain will not automatically cancel the shuttle. If organisers close the festival field because of unsafe conditions, updates will appear on the festival website and on notices at Bay C. Tickets bought before a cancellation will be refunded through the festival office, rather than by drivers. Visitors leaving belongings on a shuttle should contact the office with the journey time and a description of the item. Items are kept for seven days before they are passed to the town's lost-property service.

texts.title: Bramwell Visitor Centre: information for new employees
paragraphs: Welcome to Bramwell Visitor Centre. On your first working day, arrive at the staff entrance at 8.45 a.m., fifteen minutes before induction begins. The public entrance will still be locked. Bring photographic identification and your bank details so that the administrator can complete your employment record. Your supervisor will issue a temporary access pass. A permanent pass will be supplied after your photograph has been taken during the induction. Never lend either kind of pass to another person, including a colleague.

Induction takes place in the training room and covers emergency procedures, customer care and the booking system. Employees who will handle payments must also complete a separate till workshop before they serve customers independently. This workshop is held every Wednesday afternoon. Until they have completed it, new employees may observe an experienced cashier but may not process payments themselves. The centre provides written guidance for reference; reading it does not replace attendance at either training session. Ask your supervisor if the scheduled time conflicts with your shift.

Each employee is allocated a locker in the staff room. Store bags and outdoor coats there before starting work; the reception desk must remain clear. The centre supplies a polo shirt, which must be worn during public opening hours, but employees provide their own plain black trousers and suitable closed shoes. Your locker key must be returned when your employment ends. Personal phones should remain in lockers during shifts. Employees may check them during breaks, provided they do so away from areas used by visitors.

The weekly rota is published on the staff noticeboard each Friday. A request to exchange shifts must be agreed by both employees and approved by the supervisor before the exchange takes place. Writing a different name on the rota is not sufficient. If illness prevents you from working, call the duty manager at least one hour before your shift begins. Do not rely on a text message or a message sent through another employee. Planned appointments should be discussed as early as possible so that cover can be arranged.

All accidents and near misses must be entered in the incident register, even when nobody has been injured. The register is kept in the manager's office. The duty manager will explain the reporting procedure and arrange any immediate assistance. A review meeting will be held after your first four weeks. Keep a note of tasks you would like further help with and bring it to this meeting.

texts.title: Westmoor Council: borrowing portable equipment
paragraphs: Council employees may borrow portable projectors, audio recorders and presentation screens from the equipment store for work-related activities. The store is open between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. on weekdays. Equipment must be requested through the internal booking form at least two working days before collection. A request is not confirmed until the store sends an approval email. To avoid duplicate bookings, nominate one member of your team to submit the form. The equipment cannot be lent to friends or used for private events.

Collect the equipment in person and show your staff identification. If another employee will collect it on your behalf, their name must appear on the booking form. The assistant will check the contents of the case with the collector and record any existing damage on the collection sheet. A projector case includes a power cable, a connection cable and a remote control. Batteries are provided for the remote control. Employees should test the equipment before leaving the store, since an available replacement may be harder to obtain once they have travelled to a venue.

The standard borrowing period is three working days. Equipment is due back by 3 p.m. on the final day stated in the approval email. To request a longer period, contact the store before that deadline. An extension is possible only if the equipment has not been reserved by another team. Do not assume that a delayed meeting automatically extends the loan. If a piece of equipment develops a fault, stop using it and telephone the store. Do not attempt repairs, open the casing or arrange an outside repair company yourself.

Carry projectors in their supplied cases and keep drinks away from all electrical equipment. Screens should be transported by two people when stairs cannot be avoided. Equipment must never be left overnight in a vehicle, even if the vehicle is locked. At a venue, the borrowing team is responsible for arranging secure storage whenever equipment is unattended. Keep the collection sheet with the case so that the item number and store contact details can be found quickly if a problem occurs. Report loss or theft to the store immediately.

On return, the assistant checks the equipment and every accessory against the collection sheet. Allow about ten minutes for this inspection rather than leaving the case at the door. Borrowers will be asked to replace missing accessories, but ordinary wear is not treated as damage. There is no charge for an approved loan. Repeated late returns may lead to borrowing privileges being suspended.

sections.title: Section 3 — A longer text of general interest

texts.title: What makes a neighbourhood repair café last?
paragraphs: A. When a small library in Fenbridge announced its first repair café, the organisers imagined a quiet afternoon with a few broken lamps and loose chair legs. Instead, forty residents arrived, carrying everything from torn jackets to a radio that had been silent for years. The event's popularity seemed to prove that people wanted an alternative to throwing possessions away. However, a crowded first session says little about whether a project will still be running a year later. Interviews with the Fenbridge volunteers reveal that the difficult work began after the visitors had gone home: sorting records, discussing repairs that had failed, and deciding what the group could realistically offer next time.

B. One early change concerned how visitors understood the service. Some had expected to leave an item at the door and return later to collect it. The volunteers wanted a different relationship. Their purpose was to work alongside owners and explain the process, so that a successful repair might also build confidence. They rewrote their publicity to make participation clear. Visitors were asked to stay with their belongings, describe the fault and, where safe, help with simple steps. There was no guarantee of success. An item might be unsuitable for repair at the café, or an essential part might be unavailable. Setting these expectations reduced disappointment without reducing the number of people who came.

C. Matching knowledge to demand was another challenge. The first volunteer team included several people who could repair clothing but only one with experience of electrical appliances. As a result, a queue formed for electrical advice while the sewing table sometimes stood empty. Advertising simply for 'more volunteers' did little to correct the imbalance. The coordinator began recording the categories of items brought in and used those records to recruit particular skills. A local college helped the group find two retired technicians. They did not make the café capable of repairing every device, but they reduced its dependence on a single person and made it easier to offer useful advice when a repair could not be completed.

D. The organisers also learned that a pleasant room was not necessarily a practical workshop. The library's original event space was welcoming, yet its tables were too small for larger objects and its sockets were concentrated along one wall. Trailing cables made movement awkward. The group moved to a meeting room with heavier tables, clearer routes between work areas and better access to power. A separate desk was used to register arrivals before items reached a repair table. This helped volunteers identify jobs outside their agreed scope and explain the likely wait. A donation jar covered some small expenses, but contributions remained optional; nobody received priority because they gave more money.

E. Safety rules were sometimes mistaken for reluctance to help. One resident was frustrated when volunteers declined to work on a damaged microwave. The coordinator explained that enthusiasm alone could not make every repair appropriate in a public session. The group developed a written list of excluded work, including microwave repairs and alterations to gas appliances. Volunteers checked the condition of each item before starting and stopped if a new risk became apparent. This procedure did not eliminate all uncertainty. It did, however, give them a shared basis for decisions, rather than leaving each person to improvise under pressure from a waiting owner. Clear boundaries protected the volunteers' confidence as well as the visitors' safety.

F. Measuring the café's contribution proved less straightforward than counting the objects that left in working order. Some visitors learned how to maintain an item even when it could not be repaired that afternoon. Others discovered that a missing part could be ordered and returned at a later session. Recording both outcomes was more informative than marking every unfinished job as a failure. The team began asking visitors what they had learned and whether they intended to keep using the item. These answers were useful but had limitations: people might express an intention that they never carried out. The organisers therefore avoided claiming a precise quantity of waste prevented from these conversations alone. They reported completed repairs separately from advice and learning outcomes.

G. After a year, Fenbridge's café met monthly rather than every weekend, as some residents had initially requested. A monthly schedule gave volunteers time to rest, obtain parts and prepare for the next session. A monthly schedule was useful here, but it would not be right for every neighbourhood. Responsibilities were shared: one person coordinated bookings, another maintained supplies, and a third kept the records. The arrangement was less dramatic than a large launch event, but it was easier to sustain. Other neighbourhoods considering a similar project could copy the timetable or the registration form, yet local demand and available skills would still differ. The most useful lesson was not a fixed recipe. It was the value of reviewing experience honestly and adapting the project before a small difficulty became a reason for volunteers to leave.

tests.title: Original General Training diagnostic 2: deliveries, working life and a town sound archive

texts.title: Harbour Parcel Hub: information for customers
paragraphs: Harbour Parcel Hub receives deliveries for residents who cannot be at home when a courier calls. Register online before using the address; registration itself is free. The hub accepts parcels from all couriers, but it does not accept fresh food, live plants or items requiring a signature from a named professional. Customers remain responsible for checking these restrictions with the sender before ordering.

When a parcel arrives, the hub sends a collection message containing a locker number and an access code. Parcels remain in a locker for two days. After that, staff move them to the service desk; they are not immediately returned to the sender. The original code stops working when the parcel is moved, so customers must bring photographic identification to collect it from a member of staff.

The lockers can be reached between 6 a.m. and 11 p.m. every day. The service desk opens from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Monday to Saturday, and is closed on Sundays. A customer arriving outside desk hours cannot ask the security guard to release a stored parcel. The guard looks after the building and has no access to the parcel records.

If someone else is collecting for you, complete the authorisation form available in your account. Your collector must show the confirmation from that form and their own identification at the service desk. Forwarding your original collection message is not sufficient. Do not share access codes with neighbours: the hub cannot establish who entered a locker using a valid code.

Delivery storage costs £2 per parcel for the first four days, including the time spent in a locker. After four days, a further £1 is charged for each additional day. Paying a charge online does not extend the locker period. Parcels that remain uncollected for ten days are returned, and customers receive an email explaining when this will happen.

For a damaged parcel, ask staff to record the visible damage before you leave the desk. They can provide a dated collection record, but claims about the goods must go to the seller. The hub does not open packages to inspect their contents. Keep the outer packaging until the seller has told you whether it is needed.

texts.title: Marlow Shore Walk: arrangements for Saturday visitors
paragraphs: The Marlow Heritage Group offers a guided shore walk on the first Saturday of each month. The route follows the old harbour wall before crossing a stretch of exposed sand. Visitors learn how boats once reached the warehouses. The walk is designed for adults and children aged eight or over; every child must stay with an accompanying adult throughout the visit.

Book a place through the group's website. The guide needs the names of everyone attending because the group is limited to eighteen people. Payment confirms a place; an unfinished booking form does not. A waiting list is available when all places have gone. Waiting-list visitors should come only after receiving an offer and paying, since the guide cannot add people at the meeting point.

A full refund is available if you cancel before noon on the Thursday before the walk. After that, you may transfer your booking to another person but cannot receive a refund. Tell the office the replacement visitor's name before Friday evening. If the group cancels the event, all booking fees are refunded automatically, regardless of when visitors booked.

Meet outside the ticket office twenty minutes before the advertised departure. A board beside its door shows the day's tide information. The route can change if birds are nesting near the usual crossing, even when weather and tides are suitable. The guide will explain any change before the group leaves; visitors should not follow an old route map on their own.

Wear footwear suitable for wet sand and bring a waterproof jacket. Boots are not supplied, and ordinary trainers may become soaked. The group lends lightweight walking poles without charge, but these must be requested when booking. The tour does not enter deep water. People uncertain about managing uneven ground should contact the office before paying rather than relying on the description alone.

There is no visitor parking beside the ticket office. Bus 14 stops outside the museum, a short walk from the meeting point. Allow time to cross the road at the marked crossing; the harbour entrance is used by delivery vehicles. A small café near the museum opens before the morning walks, but it is operated independently and its purchases are not included in the tour fee.

texts.title: Glenford Meal Service: dispatch guidance for new staff
paragraphs: Glenford prepares boxed lunches for local workplaces. Dispatch staff check completed orders, pack them and pass them to drivers. Lena is responsible for equipment and can arrange a replacement scanner or trolley. Omar manages stock records and investigates differences between the recorded and actual quantities. Priya deals with customer requests, including changes to delivery times. Jules coordinates drivers and vehicle routes. Contact the person responsible instead of sending a general message that several colleagues may assume someone else will answer.

At the start of a shift, read the dispatch board and check the temperature display in the packing room. Record the number on the daily sheet even when it is within the permitted range shown beside the display. If it is outside that range, tell the shift supervisor and wait for instructions before moving any food. A previous worker's entry is not a substitute for your own check. Keep drinks on the shelf outside the packing area, away from boxes and printed labels.

Every lunch box has an order label showing its destination and any special dietary requirement. Match the label against the order on the scanner before sealing the outer container. Staff must never replace a meal marked for a dietary requirement with a different meal on their own initiative, even when a driver is waiting. Ask the kitchen supervisor to approve and record an alternative. An item that looks similar may contain different ingredients, and a handwritten change can be missed by the person receiving it.

Count the boxes for each destination before transferring them to a driver. If your total differs from the scanner total, count again with a colleague before reporting the discrepancy to Omar. Do not alter the stock figure simply to make the two totals agree. The driver signs only after the count has been confirmed. Keep completed destinations apart from unfinished ones; placing both on a shared trolley makes it harder for the next worker to identify which checks have already been carried out.

If a scanner fails, stop using it and tell Lena. Continue on a paper sheet from the drawer beside the dispatch board; write the order number, quantity and your initials. When a replacement arrives, enter those records before processing additional orders electronically. Never enter the same order twice to test whether the replacement works. At the end of the shift, put the paper sheet in the marked tray so that the supervisor can compare it with the electronic record.

texts.title: Henslow Services: paid learning leave and course support
paragraphs: Henslow employees may apply for support for a course relevant to their current work or an agreed future role. Support is not limited to managers, and part-time employees may apply. The learning team considers the course's relevance, staffing needs and the available budget. A course that interests an employee personally will not automatically qualify. Discuss the purpose with your line manager before completing the application, but remember that this conversation is not formal approval.

Applications must include the course dates, fees, expected learning outcomes and an explanation of how the learning will be used. The learning team aims to reply within five working days after receiving all the information. If something is missing, that period starts when the missing information arrives, not when the first form was sent. Applicants should therefore allow time for questions. An approaching provider deadline does not require the team to approve an incomplete application.

Employees must receive written approval before enrolling on a course for which they want financial support. Approval states the maximum fee contribution and any paid leave agreed. Courses can take place during working hours or in an employee's own time. Approval of a fee does not by itself grant time away from work. The employee and line manager must agree how essential duties will be covered before any absence is entered on the rota.

After finishing a supported course, submit a receipt and a short account of what was learned. The finance team needs the receipt before reimbursing the approved fee. The account should identify one realistic application at work; it is not an examination, and there is no requirement to report that every part of the course was useful. The learning team uses these accounts when considering future applications, but does not publish individual comments with employees' names.

If a provider cancels a course, contact the provider about a refund and inform the learning team immediately. Return any refunded amount that the company has already reimbursed. If you decide to withdraw, speak to the learning team before cancelling: an agreed replacement date may be possible. Unused learning leave cannot be carried forward as extra holiday. Keep your line manager informed about any change that affects cover, even when the provider deals directly with the learning team.

sections.title: Section 3 — A longer text of general interest

texts.title: Listening to a changing town
paragraphs: A. When the town of Bellmere began a sound archive, its first volunteers imagined collecting noises that were already disappearing: an old ferry bell, a mechanical ticket machine and the shutters of a traditional shop. These recordings attracted interest, but a visit to a school changed the project's direction. Pupils wanted to record the sounds they heard every morning, including a pedestrian crossing and voices near a sports hall. Such suggestions challenged the assumption that only unusual or historic sounds deserved attention. An ordinary sound may be so familiar that residents stop noticing it, yet its disappearance can alter their experience of a place. The archive consequently began documenting everyday surroundings as well as rare survivors.

B. Where to record was a less obvious decision than it first appeared. Most early volunteers lived near the centre, so the collection quickly accumulated market stalls, buses and busy shopping streets. Quiet housing areas and the industrial edge were scarcely represented. The project introduced a simple recording grid and invited volunteers to suggest locations in each part of town. This did not require an identical number of recordings everywhere: a railway junction and a residential lane offer different conditions. It did require the team to recognise the limits of its own movements. A believable account of the town needs more than the places its most active contributors happen to visit.

C. A recording without useful notes can be surprisingly difficult to interpret. What sounds like rain may actually be a kitchen extractor heard from outside. Volunteers therefore record the date, time, location and known source, and note conditions that might influence what can be heard. They also label uncertainty rather than quietly turning a guess into a fact. If a distant noise cannot be identified, the description says so. An original note is retained when a later listener suggests a different explanation, with the new interpretation added separately. This makes disagreement visible and allows future users to judge how firmly an interpretation is supported, instead of inheriting a confident label whose origin has been lost.

D. The team also decided that making a recording possible did not necessarily make it appropriate to share. Under the project's own rules, volunteers ask permission before recording an identifiable conversation for publication. A busy street recording may be retained while a private exchange captured clearly in the foreground is removed. Contributors can request that a recording be withdrawn from the public collection, although this may leave a gap in an exhibition already being planned. These decisions sometimes slow the work, but the coordinators consider that preferable to surprising residents with material they did not expect to be published. The archive's policy is explained during training; volunteers are not asked to infer it from the behaviour of other recordists.

E. The first public exhibition presented many recordings through loudspeakers in one room. Visitors found it hard to separate them and often left quickly. At the next exhibition, headphones allowed people to compare two recordings of the same location made at different times. A short written introduction explained what to listen for without claiming that everyone would hear the same thing. School groups could discuss their impressions before reading the volunteers' notes. Some noticed changes in traffic; others attended to voices or the spaces between sounds. The revised design did more than reduce noise in the room. It turned listening from a stream of unrelated impressions into an opportunity to ask a question and compare possible answers.

F. Counting recordings is easy; deciding what they reveal is harder. A quiet recording of a square on one morning does not show that the square is generally quiet. Work schedules, weather and the position of a microphone can change the result. The team now keeps repeated recordings with their conditions clearly marked, rather than choosing a single clip as the definitive sound of a place. It also distinguishes the number of website downloads from evidence that people have used a recording to learn something. A teacher's description of a classroom comparison can show a use that a download total cannot. Neither measure alone provides a complete account of the archive's value.

G. The collection will need attention long after its first funding period. Two copies of each original file are kept at separate locations, and a technician checks whether the files can still be opened. Public versions may be shortened, but the original is retained so that later questions are not limited by the first editor's interests. The town will keep changing, and future listeners may care about details that seem unimportant now. Preserving those possibilities involves both technical maintenance and clear records of editorial choices. The point is not to freeze Bellmere into a single authentic soundtrack. It is to give people material with which they can compare changes and question how accounts of the town were assembled.

drills.title: Original drill: a shared garden — views, headings and information

texts.title: Starting a shared garden
paragraphs: A. A neighbourhood garden works best when its members know what they have agreed to do. Before buying tools, a new group should decide how watering, maintenance and access will be shared. A simple written agreement can prevent disagreements later. An elaborate website is not essential at this stage; a noticeboard and a contact list can be sufficient. The first priority should be clear expectations rather than impressive publicity. New members should be able to ask questions without feeling that they are challenging the organisers.

B. It would be a mistake to use every available corner for growing vegetables. Shared gardens should also include quiet seating for people who want to enjoy the space without cultivating a plot. Paths must allow visitors to move safely, and tool storage should be accessible. At our garden, a sheltered bench has become a meeting place for neighbours who previously had little reason to speak to one another. A garden can strengthen social connections as well as provide fresh food.

C. Expanding too quickly can make a successful project fragile. Starting with a few beds gives volunteers time to learn how much work they can manage. The group can add more when it has enough regular helpers. This cautious approach may look less exciting than opening a large site at once, but it can make the difference between a lasting garden and an abandoned space. Occasional reviews should consider both the condition of the plants and the workload of the people caring for them.

texts.title: Rooms at Marlow House
paragraphs: Three rooms at Marlow House are available to staff. Room A, the Cedar Room, seats eight around a single table. It has no presentation equipment and is intended for small discussions. Its ground-floor location provides step-free access. Food must not be brought into Cedar because the same room is used for document conservation at other times. Reserve it at least one day ahead through the office coordinator.

Room B, the Harbour Room, seats twenty and includes a fixed projector. It is the only room available after six in the evening. Light refreshments are permitted, but users must clear them away afterwards. Harbour is on the first floor, which can be reached by lift. Evening users collect a temporary building pass from the coordinator before four in the afternoon and return it the next working day.

Room C, the Willow Room, is a ground-floor workshop with movable tables and washable flooring. It seats twelve and is suitable for practical activities involving water-based paint. It has a sink but no projector. Bookings cannot be made for evenings. Users must return tables to their marked positions and rinse the sink before leaving. Report damaged furniture to the office coordinator instead of trying to repair it.

drills.title: Original drill: volunteering — summary, notes, table and flow chart

texts.title: Oakfield Run: volunteer preparation
paragraphs: Volunteers for the Oakfield Run must register through the event website by Monday. The coordinator then sends a confirmation email containing a training link. Volunteers watch the training video and complete the online safety quiz before collecting their kit. Those who pass the quiz receive a collection code; anyone who does not pass can watch the video again and retry. Present the code when collecting the kit from the sports hall on Friday.

The kit contains a yellow vest, a route map and an emergency contact card. Volunteers bring their own waterproof jacket and lunch. The organisers provide drinking water at each station. On event day, all volunteers attend a briefing at seven in the morning at the sports hall. After the briefing, they travel to their assigned stations. The event vehicle takes volunteers to the two most distant stations; others walk to theirs.

Station assignments are listed in the confirmation email. At the bridge station, volunteers start at eight in the morning and finish at noon. At the park station, the shift starts at nine and ends at one in the afternoon. Volunteers must not exchange stations without the coordinator's approval. Before leaving, each station returns its route map and emergency contact card to the finish tent; the yellow vest may be kept.

texts.title: Alder Library: the ground floor
paragraphs: The ground floor of Alder Library has a central corridor running north from the main entrance. Five rooms open directly onto the corridor. On the west side, the room nearest the entrance is the returns room, where borrowers leave items when the service desk is busy. The next west-side room is the study room, and the last, at the north end, is the archive. Visitors require staff permission to enter the archive.

There are two rooms on the east side. The café is nearest the entrance, directly opposite the returns room. Farther north, the children's room is opposite the study room. The archive has no room opposite it. A staff exit is at the northern end of the corridor and must not be used by visitors. Toilets are on the first floor and therefore do not appear on this ground-floor plan. There are no rooms between those described here.

drills.title: Original drill: borrowing a sewing machine — short answers

texts.title: Stitch Library: machine loans
paragraphs: Members of Stitch Library can borrow a sewing machine for home use. Before their first loan, they must attend an introduction at the sewing desk. Bring a small piece of cotton to practise threading and stitching. The instructor provides thread and demonstrates the controls. Members who already sew must still attend, because the machines have particular operating instructions. There is no charge for the introduction.

Loans last six days. Each machine is supplied with a pedal, a power cable and a printed guide. The case must be kept closed during transport. Use a brush to remove loose thread after sewing; cleaning sprays are not permitted. If the needle breaks, switch off the machine and contact the lending desk. Members must not replace it themselves. Returns are accepted at the sewing desk, rather than the general book-return slot.

Bookings open every Tuesday. Reserve by calling the lending desk or speaking to staff in person; machine bookings are not available online. A refundable deposit of £20 is collected when the machine is issued. It is returned after staff have checked the machine and its accessories. Members who want to cancel should give at least twelve hours' notice so that the machine can be offered to someone else.

questions.explanation: Cotton names the material; the instructor provides the thread.

drills.title: Original drill: cycle-parking passes — facts, exceptions and response limits

sections.title: A short notice — information and response limits

texts.title: Hillford Station: enclosed cycle parking
paragraphs: Hillford Council offers monthly passes for the enclosed cycle park beside the station. Both town residents and people who work in Hillford may apply. Applicants must provide evidence of their home or work address. The pass is personal and must not be lent to a colleague. It covers access to the cycle park, not travel on trains or buses.

Pass holders can enter at any hour using the electronic gate. Buying a pass does not reserve an individual space or guarantee that a space will be available. If the enclosure is full, use the outdoor racks; do not leave a bicycle in the entrance or against another bicycle. The outdoor racks do not require a pass.

The council records how many passes are active, but does not ask applicants about their usual journeys. Notices about maintenance are sent to the email address given on the application. Keep that address current so that you receive information about any temporary closure.

Report a lost pass through your online account. Staff will cancel the old pass before issuing a replacement. During a planned closure, temporary outdoor racks are available beside the west gate. Bring your own lock for these racks; locks are not supplied.

drills.title: Original drill: print-proof requests — negation, missing information and response limits

sections.title: A short notice — information and response limits

texts.title: Willow Printworks: requesting a proof copy
paragraphs: Before ordering a large print run, employees can ask Willow Printworks for a proof: a sample used to check the document. Send the final file and the order number at least three working days before the proof is needed. Approval from a department manager does not shorten this notice period. The print team cannot promise an earlier date simply because the final printing deadline is close.

Choose either an electronic proof or a paper proof on the request form. Both show the intended layout, but only the paper version allows you to examine the printed colour. The form does not record why an employee chose a particular format. Staff may request a second proof after making changes, using the same order number and clearly marking the new file.

Documents marked confidential are not left on the open collection shelf. A member of the print team checks the recipient's identification and hands over the paper proof in person. The recipient must be the employee named on the form; a colleague cannot collect a confidential proof on that employee's behalf.

Ordinary paper proofs are placed in the cabinet beside reception. Each envelope shows its order number. Check that number before taking anything, and notify the team if the envelope is missing. Reception staff can contact the team but do not approve changes to a document.
